I've read extensively on the era and have argued often about why the Allies "made a deal with the Devil." Revisionism being what it is, a lot of contemporary historians are prone to say that the Russians were innocent of aggression in comparison to Nazi Germany and furthermore that Britain was concerned about a full Russo-German alliance. I generally argue against both of these points, and this article does touch on some facts that support my view.

On the first, I'm led to believe that the U.S., specifically due to FDR, were instrumental in keeping the Allies from imposing any sort of sanctions against Russia. The reason for potential sanctions touches on the second, or Russian aggression - in Finland, the Baltic States, Poland, and Romania, the latter of which included areas not guaranteed in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. The Allies were willing to go to war over Poland alone.

In my view, FDR (and later Churchill) shrewdly recognized the value of Russian appeasement, specifically as a "deal with the Russian problem later" tactic. We see this again with Truman, who carried on FDR's vision, putting Europe first (the Marshall Plan, Berlin Airlift, etc.) before Asia (firing MacArthur), mirroring also the strategic choices made during WWII. U.S. pressure (and Chamberlain's inability to be aggressive) therefore likely influenced how the situation developed.

Stalin was no saint and led to the devastation of his countryman, to be sure. Yet the idea that Russian blood was enough is ridiculous, completing ignoring the logistical support and supplies afforded to him through Allied efforts. Quite simply, the idea of a Russo-German alliance over-estimates Russian strength. Furthermore, Hitler nearly worshiped Mussolini and entertained many of his ambitions; in fact, it was the Balkan question that ultimately stalled any further Russo-German treaties.

Hitler had written about his plans for Eastern Europe well before coming to power and Stalin was surely aware of this; the belief that two men, so ideologically disparate and paranoid, would be able to work together is a stretch by any means. Churchill can be lumped into this as he always preferred indirect invasions - Gallipoli in WW1, and in WW2 Sicily - and thus delayed the opening of the Western Front by one year. Obviously this caused a lot of issues for Stalin.

I could go on and talk about other issues, like the fate of the Middle East esp. Persia/Iran with regards to this article and the arguments above, but this is a good starting point. Suffice it to say that neither the old nor the revised histories tell the full truth; there was a lot of political maneuvering then as there is now.

Sources:

Richard Evans's The Third Reich Trilogy

William Manchester's American Caesar and The Last Lion

David McCullough's Truman

Jean Edward Smith's FDR
